wordings: Chronic pancreatitis can occasionally show a focal, mass-like enlargement, usually in the head of the pancreas.
A focal, mass-like enlargement can occasionally occur in chronic pancreatitis, usually in the pancreatic head.
The pancreatic head is also a predominant site for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Mass-forming chronic pancreatitis (MFCP) can resemble PDAC on CT or MRI.
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) also predominantly occurs in the pancreatic head, and mass-forming chronic pancreatitis (MFCP) can look similar on CT or MRI.
No single imaging feature reliably separates MFCP from PDAC; the combination of findings that are present or absent matters.
Distinguishing MFCP from PDAC depends on the combination of imaging findings present or absent, rather than any single reliable imaging feature.

A pancreatic duct that narrows smoothly as it passes through a mass, without an abrupt or complete blockage, favors inflammation. This duct-penetrating sign is best seen with magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP).

Smooth narrowing of the pancreatic duct through a mass, without abrupt or complete obstruction, favors an inflammatory mass. The duct-penetrating sign is best seen with magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP).
Mass-forming chronic pancreatitis (MFCP) is likely to show diffuse spotted or coarse calcifications in pancreatic tissue, or ductal calcifications, together with the duct-penetrating sign.
In mass-forming chronic pancreatitis (MFCP), diffuse spotted or coarse pancreatic tissue calcifications, or ductal calcifications, are likely to occur together with a duct-penetrating sign.
Complete pancreatic duct blockage by a mass, or arterial encasement by a soft-tissue mass, is more likely with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) than with MFCP.
Compared with MFCP, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is more likely to show complete pancreatic duct obstruction by a mass or arterial encasement by a soft-tissue mass.
MFCP can resemble PDAC on CT or MRI. No single imaging feature reliably distinguishes them; the combination of findings present or absent matters.
Because MFCP can look like PDAC on CT or MRI, their distinction depends on the combination of imaging findings present or absent. No single imaging feature reliably separates them.
Focal autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP) usually shows uniform enhancement on the portal-venous phase of CT.
On portal-venous phase CT, focal autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP) usually enhances uniformly.
Focal AIP usually shows smooth pancreatic duct narrowing without an abrupt cutoff, only mild widening of the upstream main duct (5 mm or less), and no proximal pancreatic atrophy.
Smooth pancreatic duct narrowing without an abrupt cutoff, mild upstream main-duct dilatation (5 mm or less), and no proximal pancreatic atrophy are usually seen together in focal AIP.
Focal AIP can still resemble pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
Focal AIP can mimic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
